turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, September twenty-fourth. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Morocco just voted overnight, and it's a genuine political shake-up — let's get straight into it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: PAM comes out on top.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Authenticity and Modernity Party takes the most seats in Wednesday's parliamentary election — ninety-seven of three hundred ninety-five. RNI, outgoing PM Akhannouch's party, drops to sixty-six, Istiqlal's at sixty-five, and the moderate-Islamist PJD more than quadruples, from thirteen seats in twenty twenty-one to fifty-four.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That PJD jump is the real story though — what's driving it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Youth unemployment, mostly, with twenty-thirty World Cup construction spending visible everywhere and jobs still not following. Turnout was just thirty-eight percent, the lowest since two thousand seven — so this reads as a protest surge as much as a PAM mandate. Coalition talks start now, and PAM has no obvious majority partner.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any read on who PAM actually governs with?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nobody knows yet, and that's the risk — PAM ran on an anti-corruption, cost-of-living platform, but it has no natural coalition partner at that seat count. A PJD-flavored government would be the first real Islamist-led cabinet since the twenty-eleven constitution, and markets in Casablanca are already pricing policy uncertainty into bank and telecom names.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any early reaction from Rabat itself?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The palace has stayed quiet so far, which is itself notable — past coalition talks got royal signaling almost immediately. The silence reads as the king waiting to see whether PAM can actually assemble a workable majority before weighing in.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Watch that space. Next — the Iran track actually moved this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Three hours of indirect US-Iran talks in New York, Qatar, Pakistan and Egypt mediating — the first contact since the ceasefire broke down back in June. Iran's tabled a roadmap: up to a sixty-day regionwide ceasefire and a phased Strait of Hormuz reopening, in exchange for the US lifting its naval blockade.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Washington's answer?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Not yet. Trump's holding the blockade until Iran shows, quote, sufficient goodwill. No breakthrough — but it's the first actual roadmap either side has put on paper since June, and it's exactly what's moving this morning's oil tape, which we'll get to.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: US Business — M&A first.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Copart's tender for ACV Auctions is closing in — ten dollars fifty a share cash, a forty-five point four percent premium, valuing the deal near one point nine billion. No financing condition, offer expires September thirtieth, expected to close by year-end.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And two earnings prints today that actually matter for the consumer read — Costco after the close, Darden before the open.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Costco's fiscal Q4 — Street wants ninety-four point eight six billion in revenue, up ten percent, and six fifty-five adjusted EPS, up twelve. August comps already ran plus ten point seven in the US, so the bar's high. Darden's the more interesting print — consensus two-oh-six EPS on three point two one billion, and everyone's watching the Olive Garden-versus-LongHorn gap, which blew wide open last quarter: Olive Garden comps up two point four, LongHorn up nine point five. If that spread holds, it's a real signal on where the consumer's trading down to.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: International — a central bank and a labor dispute.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: SARB hiked twenty-five basis points to seven point two five percent — unanimous vote, its second hike this year. Governor Kganyago's citing four point four percent August CPI, the Mideast conflict, Saudi export disruption from the Yemen fighting, and the Russia-Ukraine war. He sees headline inflation above five percent into early twenty twenty-seven.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Uruguay's trying to end that port strike.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The labor ministry's floated a settlement on the Montevideo container dispute — twenty-one guaranteed work days plus a one-off payment of roughly six hundred ninety to twelve fifty dollars per worker. It's Katoen Natie against the dockworkers' union Supra, a fight running since January, with a seventy-two-hour stoppage in August and a fresh strike just last Monday. Neither side's signed yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Nobody's actually closing anything this morning. Noted. Markets.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One more before we go there — worth flagging the read-through. A SARB hike into an already-fragile rand, a Uruguayan government trying to buy labor peace with a four-figure check per worker — both are central authorities spending real credibility to avoid a bigger blowup later. That's the emerging pattern.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And today the tape actually earns a full segment. Wednesday's close: the ten-year Treasury yield jumped fifteen to seventeen basis points to five point one one percent — the highest since July two thousand seven. Nineteen years.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually did that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A hotter-than-expected business-activity and cost report, the kind that reads as sticky-inflation evidence rather than noise. It dragged equities with it — Nasdaq down one point one percent to twenty-six thousand nine thirty-six, S&P off point eight to seventy-seven-oh-six, Dow down point seven to fifty-one thousand five eleven. Everything else — FTSE, DAX, Hang Seng, Shanghai — is on the Markets tab; nothing there cleared the bar today except WTI.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which did what?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Up two point four percent to ninety-two seventy-one a barrel, purely on the Hormuz-reopening uncertainty from the story we just covered — the market's not pricing the roadmap succeeding yet. Gold fell one point two percent on the stronger dollar and the hawkish yield read.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So which is the real story — the yield or the oil?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The yield, decisively. A nineteen-year high on the ten-year changes the mortgage math, the corporate-refinancing math, and the Fed's whole runway, all at once — an oil bid on a single day's geopolitics is noise by comparison. The question now is whether five percent becomes the new floor investors have to underwrite, not just a spike to trade around.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this the kind of move that forces the new Fed chair's hand?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It tightens the corridor either way. Warsh takes over discounting supply-side energy shocks, but a demand-and-cost-driven yield spike like this one is exactly the data he can't wave off — if the next print confirms the cost pressure, the market's going to have to unwind some of the cuts it's already priced for twenty twenty-seven. That's the real tail risk sitting under this morning's number.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does that do to the earnings-season setup, with Costco and Darden landing today?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It raises the discount rate everyone's using to value the forward guidance, which matters more for a growth name like Costco than a value name like Darden. If yields hold near five percent through the print, even a clean beat gets a smaller multiple reward than it would have a month ago — the bar isn't just the number, it's the number against a materially higher cost of capital.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Uncomfortable Thursday. Deep Dive.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This week's Economist cover essay is the one worth chewing on — Trump just dropped his demand to actually own Greenland.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: After eighteen months of threatening it — including not ruling out force?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly. The US, Denmark and Greenland signed a security pact Friday, timed to UN General Assembly week — it expands the American footprint at Pituffik Space Base and opens two new access points, Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east. Overflight and landing rights island-wide, explicit undersea access, and no end date on the agreement.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But not ownership.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Not ownership. And the Economist's framing is the interesting part — the annexation threat itself did lasting diplomatic damage that a, quote, modest improvement pact doesn't undo. This wasn't costless posturing; it's a case study in how a maximalist opening bid can poison the well even when you settle for less.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual evidence the damage stuck?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Polling, mostly, and it's stark. Pew found only twenty-one percent of Americans favored a Greenland takeover in January, fifty-eight percent opposed — this never had domestic political cover even while it was being pursued. In Greenland itself, roughly eighty-five percent opposed joining the US, and all five parties in its parliament jointly called the annexation talk, quote, unacceptable to friends and allies in a defense alliance. The EU, UK, Norway and Canada all publicly closed ranks behind Denmark.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Trump reportedly threatened Denmark's European neighbors too?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A twenty-five percent tariff threat on several European countries if Copenhagen didn't cede the territory — that's the coercion piece the Economist argues hardened, not softened, Denmark's position, and it's part of why the allied backlash outlasted the actual ask.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now — the part your listener actually cares about. Greenland sits on one of the last untapped critical-minerals frontiers on earth.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and that track is separate and still unsigned. Trump's floated a rare-earth rights framework alongside the security pact; the administration's already committed ten billion toward a roughly twelve-billion critical-minerals stockpile, and the Export-Import Bank issued a hundred-twenty-million-dollar loan letter of interest to Critical Metals Corp for the Tanbreez rare-earth mine.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the security pact is the wedge, and the minerals deal is what actually matters to the chip and data-center supply chain.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read. Washington's trying to break China's rare-earth chokehold, and Greenland is one of maybe three places on the planet with the deposits to do it at scale. The security pact buys the access; the minerals framework, if it ever gets signed, is the actual prize — and right now it's still a letter of interest, not a mine in production.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Did Beijing say anything about the pact?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: State media flagged it within hours as evidence the US is militarizing its critical-minerals competition, not just diversifying supply. That reaction alone tells you Beijing takes the mineral track more seriously than the security language on its face suggests it should.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual timeline on a mine like Tanbreez if the minerals framework does get signed?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Years, not months — permitting, Arctic logistics, and processing capacity that barely exists outside China today. Even a fully signed framework wouldn't move real output before the end of the decade, which is the uncomfortable footnote to the whole story — the security pact is fast, the thing it's supposedly securing is slow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Costly threat, modest win, real prize still pending. Energy.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Three separate stories this week, same underlying fight — regulators and courts refusing to take a commitment at face value.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start with the one-dollar letter of credit.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: FERC declined jurisdiction Tuesday on ComEd's cancellation of the PowerHouse Hillwood transmission security agreement — that's the one-point-eight gigawatt, twenty-billion-dollar Joliet campus. Hillwood's position is that it satisfied the TSA's credit-support requirement with a one-dollar letter of credit.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A literal one dollar.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Commissioner LaCerte called it, quote, an embarrassing legal fiction — pricing that risk for less than the price of a cup of coffee. FERC punted rather than rule, so it's now sitting in front of the Northern District of Illinois. But the question underneath it is the one every interconnection queue in the country is dancing around: does a nominal megawatt commitment mean anything if the credit support behind it is essentially zero?

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: California just answered a version of that question with actual legislation.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Newsom signed the data-center oversight package Monday. On-site clean-generation incentives, mandatory water-supply assessments tied to permitting, statewide water-use reporting tied to business-license renewal — the standard direct-cost-assignment playbook we've covered before. But the sharper tool is that data centers lose their blanket CEQA exemption.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Meaning every future California campus faces discretionary environmental review.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Real schedule risk hyperscalers haven't had to price on the West Coast until now — a CEQA challenge can add a year or more before a shovel goes in the ground, and there's no cap on how many times a project can be challenged.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the third one — the RTO adder fight in New England.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Connecticut, Maine, Maryland and New Jersey filed Monday asking FERC to strip Avangrid's Central Maine Power and Versant of the point-five-percent ROE adder they get for voluntary ISO-NE membership. Small dollars — it added about six million in twenty twenty-four regional charges, with Maine ratepayers alone eating roughly seven hundred thousand of that.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Remind us what the adder actually compensates utilities for.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a return-on-equity kicker FERC created years ago to reward utilities for voluntarily joining a regional transmission organization, back when RTO membership genuinely was optional and utilities had to be bribed into the coordination benefits. Avangrid's been collecting it on the CMP and Versant books ever since.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does that matter beyond Maine?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because four states passed laws this year mandating RTO participation, which guts the "voluntary incentive" rationale FERC uses to justify the adder in the first place — the same logic FERC already used to deny the adder to California and Ohio utilities. If it falls region-wide, that's a direct rate-base hit to transmission owners right as they're asking for massive capex approval tied to data-center load growth.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And it's a template for every other RTO, not just New England.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Once one region's transmission owners lose the voluntary-incentive argument against a mandated program, every other RTO's utilities have to defend the same adder on the same shaky ground — right as they're all filing for grid-upgrade recovery tied to hyperscaler interconnection queues.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any read on how developers are actually pricing this collateral risk into new deals, given the Hillwood fight?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The early signal is credit committees asking for real letters of credit up front now, not just contractual promises — a few large developers have started publishing collateral terms in their PPA term sheets specifically to pre-empt this exact dispute. It's a small, quiet shift, but it's the market self-correcting faster than the regulators are.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A dollar that isn't collateral, an exemption that isn't automatic, an incentive that isn't voluntary. Consistent morning. Tagalog Vocab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Panandalian.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Panandalian — pansamantala, o hindi tuluyang solusyon. Mas may bigat ito kaysa sa karaniwang salitang "pansamantala," at mas madalas gamitin sa political at economic commentary, lalo na kapag binibigyang-diin na hindi pa ito ang tunay na solusyon sa ugat ng problema.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Solusyong panandalian lang ito, hindi ito ang tunay na kasagutan." Karaniwang pares nito: solusyong panandalian, ayuda panandalian, kaluwagan panandalian — lagi itong may implikasyon na darating pa ang tunay na hakbang.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Susunod — kahina-hinala.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kahina-hinala — may itsura ng mali, pero wala pang sapat na patunay. Mas malumanay at mas may dating-balita ito kumpara sa mas diretsahang "kaduda-duda," kaya mas madalas itong makikita sa court reporting at investigative journalism, kung saan kailangang mag-ingat sa pananalita hangga't hindi pa napapatunayan ang paratang.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa naman.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Kahina-hinala ang mga kontratang iyon, pero wala pa tayong sapat na ebidensya." Pareho itong mababagsak natin sa susunod na balita — parehong salita, dalawang magkaibang usapin.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Nagbago na naman ang patakaran sa Senado kung ilang boto ang kailangan para mahatulan si VP Sara Duterte.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Hindi na raw fixed sa labing-anim — depende na ngayon sa kung ilang senador-hukom ang talagang nasa korte.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anim ang nag-boycott sa botohan, pero nanalo pa rin ang bagong panuntunan, labing-tatlo kontra isa.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the record now, in English — Day twenty-nine of the trial, Wednesday: the impeachment court voted thirteen-to-one to scrap presiding officer Escudero's fixed sixteen-vote conviction threshold, adopting Senator Tulfo's motion for a dynamic two-thirds denominator based only on senator-judges actually present — excluding anyone detained, suspended, in hiding, or medically incapacitated.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Remind us what the first move was.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two episodes back the court lowered the threshold outright, to fourteen votes. This time it didn't change the number — it changed what counts as the denominator. Same direction, different mechanism: fewer senators effectively needed to convict, however you get there.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is the second time the math's moved.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is — and each move has trimmed the number of votes actually needed to convict. Six senators boycotted, including both Cayetanos, Imee Marcos, Christopher Go, Camille Villar and Robin Padilla; Escudero cast the lone dissent; Mark Villar broke from the boycotting bloc to vote yes. Whichever way this trial ends, the procedural fight over how you count to two-thirds is now as contested as the verdict itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Separately — Baste Duterte actually took the stand this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Subpoenaed testimony, Tuesday — the Davao mayor denied any knowledge that his sister, VP Sara Duterte, held an interest in GenCorp Industries, a firm that's pulled nineteen Davao City government contracts worth over thirty-three million pesos since twenty twenty. Kahina-hinala, as we just said — suspicious on its face, not yet proven.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kahina-hinala, as we just learned it — a word for exactly this kind of story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Precisely why the vocab lesson tied to it. Prosecutors will need actual paper trail evidence, not just the contract pattern, to move this from suspicious to proven — but nineteen contracts to one firm over five years is the kind of number that makes the suspicion hard to wave away.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the economy — and it's not a good week for the peso.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: S&P Global expects BSP to hike another twenty-five basis points to five point two five percent before year-end. The peso's down more than five percent against the dollar since mid-September — among the worst in Asia alongside the rupee, rupiah and baht — and S&P sees twenty twenty-six inflation averaging five point five percent, versus just one point seven last year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's BSP actually watching before it pulls the trigger on that hike?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The peso's trajectory into the next inflation print, mainly — if it keeps sliding past sixty-three, the hike stops being optional. S&P's twenty twenty-seven numbers assume the hike lands on schedule: inflation easing to three point six percent, BSP itself easing back to four point five as the currency stabilizes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And growth is taking the hit too.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: S&P cut its twenty twenty-six PH growth forecast to two point nine percent, down from four point one; ADB cut its own number to three point three, from three point eight. The PSEi fell one point one two percent to five thousand seven thirty on Wednesday — a fifth straight losing session — as rising local yields piled on top of the peso weakness. Panandalian is the operative word here — BSP's hike buys time against the peso slide, it doesn't fix the growth story underneath it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the read for anyone with peso-denominated savings right now?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Panandalian applies here too — don't treat a single BSP hike as the fix. The peso's slide is being driven as much by the dollar's broader strength this week, off that nineteen-year Treasury yield, as by anything domestic. Until that outside pressure eases, one twenty-five-basis-point move is a stopgap, not a floor.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: No storm signal today, so we'll leave weather off. Mandarin Vocab.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Today's first word is 缓解, huǎnjiě — to ease or alleviate pressure, without actually resolving it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's that different from just "fixing" something?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the contrast — 解决, jiějué, means to resolve completely; 缓解 only lessens the severity, the root cause is still sitting there. It's a formal, written-register word — 书面语 — you'll see it constantly in economic and diplomatic reporting. Common collocations: 缓解压力, ease pressure; 缓解紧张局势, ease tensions; 缓解危机, ease a crisis.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Give us the example we'll actually hear in a minute.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管美中把关税休战延长到明年一月十日，中国国内的房地产和地方债务危机还是没有缓解。 Although the US and China extended their tariff truce to January tenth next year, China's domestic property and local-government debt crisis still hasn't eased.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 让步, ràngbù.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: To make a concession, to yield — and specifically it marks one side backing down, often under pressure. Contrast it with 妥协, tuǒxié, "compromise," which implies both sides give ground toward a middle point. 让步 is one-directional. Also formal register, standard in negotiation and diplomatic coverage — you'll hear 做出让步 or 作出让步, "to make a concession," and 被迫让步, "forced to concede."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Example.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 中国在农产品采购上做出了让步，可是稀土交付进度依然落后。 China made concessions on agricultural purchases, but its rare-earth delivery schedule is still behind. Both words, straight into the China story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more thing worth flagging before we get there — what's the truce NOT covering?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Taiwan arms sales and chip export controls, both explicitly carved out as separate tracks at the summit. That tells you how much of this "deal" is actually just the parts both sides could agree to defer.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管美中把关税休战延长到明年一月十日，中国国内的房地产和地方债务危机还是没有缓解。 Although the US and China extended their tariff truce to January tenth next year, China's domestic property and local-government debt crisis still hasn't eased.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk us through what actually happened.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Xi landed in Washington Wednesday for his second Trump summit this year — a state visit running through Friday — and Bessent announced the truce, which was set to expire November tenth, is now pushed to January tenth instead. Beijing still owes deliverables from the October twenty twenty-five Busan truce: it hit its twenty-five-million-ton US soybean pledge, but it's lagging on a separate seventeen-billion-dollar agricultural commitment, and rare-earth export deliveries are running behind too.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 中国在农产品采购上做出了让步，可是稀土交付进度依然落后。 China made concessions on agricultural purchases, but its rare-earth delivery schedule is still behind.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the gap. Both sides are also working toward tariff cuts, potentially to zero, on thirty billion dollars of goods each side, and floating the bilateral Board of Trade platform for ongoing disputes going forward.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Put this through the two-speed lens for us.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Beijing's buying runway for the export lane — the fast lane that's still propping up headline growth — precisely while the domestic side keeps deflating. Land-sale revenue is down roughly sixteen percent this year, property investment's tracking negative four to negative six. A tariff truce doesn't touch local-government debt or the property overhang; it just protects the one engine currently offsetting weak domestic demand.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the lagging deliverables tell you even that engine isn't running clean.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — partial compliance on soybeans, real shortfall on the rest. 缓解, not 解决. Easing the trade friction was the achievable goal here; resolving the debt-deflation problem underneath it was never on the table this week.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Taiwan and chips are sitting right there, untouched, the whole time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Deliberately so — both sides needed a deliverable this week, and the tariff track was the one they could actually move. Taiwan arms sales and chip export controls stay exactly where they were, which means the truce is buying calm on the easiest axis while the hardest ones just keep accumulating pressure underneath. Arts.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Los Angeles first — a genuinely powerful gallery show.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Jordan Nassar opened his fifth solo show with Anat Ebgi last Friday — Describing Clouds, new multi-panel hand embroideries extending his work with tatreez, traditional Palestinian cross-stitch, in modular configurations that nod to Monir Farmanfarmaian's convertible mirror mosaics.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does that fit into what Nassar's usually doing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He's spent a decade putting tatreez — a domestic, historically women's craft — into a fine-art register without losing its politics; this show pushes it structurally, hinging panels so the geometry actually shifts as you move around the room.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the centerpiece?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A mosaic tile work called Jabalia, drawn directly from the excavated remains of a fifth-century Byzantine church at Mukheitim in Gaza. It's folk-craft abstraction grounded in an archaeological record that's itself now endangered — the work doesn't editorialize, it just insists the record existed. Runs through October thirty-first.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Met opened its season this week too, and the reviews are split.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A new Verdi Macbeth, the Met debut for director Louisa Proske, Quinn Kelsey in the title role, Lise Davidsen as Lady Macbeth. Critics across OperaWire, Parterre Box and Slippedisc converge on the same read — Kelsey's towering, vocally dominant Macbeth anchors what's otherwise a consistently involving production.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Davidsen?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Vocally sumptuous, by every account — but dramatically underpowered, missing the ambition and menace the role actually needs. A useful reminder that a starry cast doesn't guarantee a coherent staging; you can win the singing and still lose the performance.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — a serious critical reappraisal in the LRB.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Andrew O'Hagan reviews Hermione Lee's new Anita Brookner biography in this week's issue — Omelettes and Whisky: Anita Brookner's Edge. Brookner was an art historian who turned novelist at fifty-three and then published a book a year for two decades. O'Hagan uses Lee's excavation of her to argue Brookner's precision has aged far better than the lazy spinster-novelist caricature she got saddled with at the time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Overdue correction, and it fits the week — three different capacities getting reassessed on the actual merits instead of the received story about them.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nassar's tatreez, Kelsey carrying an uneven staging, Brookner outliving her own caricature — same move each time, evidence over reputation.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fair callback. Op-Eds.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: David Ignatius in the Post this week — Xi, Trump and Putin may seem immovable, but their time is passing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: All three are aging — Trump's eighty, Xi and Putin are both seventy-three — amid real succession speculation in every capital. Ignatius's point is that personalist authoritarian systems turn brittle exactly when a leader's mortality becomes an open question, so this week's UN dominance display actually masks a coming succession crisis that democracies should be planning for now, not later.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Betting on strongman mortality as a strategy is the same wishful thinking that misjudged Putin after twenty-fourteen and Xi after COVID. Autocratic successions historically produce continuity or harder-line heirs, not liberalization — and "twilight" framing risks lulling policymakers into passivity toward leaders who remain fully empowered today. History's actual track record here favors the skeptics.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece — Nate Silver, and this one's got real data behind it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Silver's argument in the Bulletin is that diesel prices, not gasoline, could crush Republicans in the heartland. The Hormuz-driven price shock — that same Iran story from the top of the show — is hitting diesel and heating oil far harder than headline gas, a combined shock of forty-eight to sixty-three percent across Iowa, Nebraska, Michigan, Kansas and Texas.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does that matter more than the gasoline number everyone's watching?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's concentrated precisely in the farm-belt Senate races the GOP needs to hold, and it maps onto exactly the states where Democrats are suddenly polling competitive — a sharper, more immediate pocketbook signal than generic approval polling. The counter is straightforward: single-commodity spikes are historically poor standalone midterm predictors, and this one could unwind well before November. The diesel-exposed states and the tight races may just be catching the same pre-existing polling volatility, not causation — and Silver himself concedes AI-driven economic anxiety could be a confounding variable he can't fully strip out.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything else pulling votes here that the diesel story alone doesn't fully capture?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Silver flags one more thing worth naming — the districts hit hardest also skew toward the exact independents who broke for Trump in twenty twenty-four on affordability, not ideology. If diesel doesn't come down before the primaries start, that's the coalition most exposed, not the base.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Hormuz story just keeps circling back today. One Good Thing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Christine Todd has polycystic kidney disease, and for months she stood outside White Sox games in Chicago wearing a homemade t-shirt and holding a banner, asking total strangers if they'd consider donating a kidney.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Somebody actually saw it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Chris Beck, a biology teacher in Virginia who'd never met her, caught the local news coverage, got tested on a whim, and turned out to be a perfect match. He'd already donated part of his liver to a stranger back in twenty twenty — this was his second time giving an organ to someone he'd never met before the operation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And they've both recovered.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Both healthy now — and they went back together to the ballpark where her search actually started, the two of them standing in the same spot where she used to hold that banner alone. That's the show. I'm Alex.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And I'm Sam. That's your Thursday — we'll see you tomorrow.
